tagline: Stone boundaries and working hayfields between two historic New Hampshire homes.
intro: The Currier & Ives Scenic Byway passes rolling countryside, covered bridges and village centers in central New Hampshire. Visit NH gives the route a length of 40 miles and points to stone walls marking old property lines, fields hayed for more than 200 years, and views of Mount Kearsarge and Pats Peak. It is a state-designated scenic byway, with eighteenth- and nineteenth-century churches and community buildings gathered in village clusters.

The route began in 1976, when the state Office of Travel and Tourism identified it as one of the Bicentennial “Yankee Trails.” It entered the Scenic and Cultural Byways Program in 1994. A community-developed corridor plan followed in 2009–2010, balancing conservation with tourism and economic development. A byway council formed in 2010 with appointed town representatives to implement and update the plan. The Currier & Ives Foundation holds the name’s registered trademark and permits its use for the byway.

Beginning at Daniel Webster’s birthplace in Franklin, the journey continues through Salisbury and Webster toward Hopkinton. In Hopkinton’s Contoocook village, the covered railroad bridge crosses the river beside the historic depot. West Hopkinton occupies the town’s more agricultural section. Henniker follows along the Contoocook, before the journey ends at the Franklin Pierce Homestead in Hillsborough.
notice: Stone walls mark former property boundaries beside fields that remain in hay production.

moments.title: Daniel Webster Birthplace
moments.text: A two-room log cabin in Franklin preserves the setting associated with Daniel Webster’s birth in 1782 and his early childhood. The restored house interprets late-eighteenth-century farm life. This is the birthplace historic site, distinct from The Elms, the family property that Webster inherited in 1829 and used as a summer home.

moments.title: Contoocook Railroad Bridge
moments.text: The covered railroad bridge crosses the Contoocook at an angle, with its central pier and abutments skewed to follow the river’s flow. The crossing was substantially rebuilt in 1889 to replace a lighter covered railroad bridge. Its double Town lattice trusses continue over the middle pier to form two spans. It is the oldest surviving covered railroad bridge in the United States. After rail service ended, the bridge became a warehouse; that use lasted until 1989, when it became public property. Preservation has relied on the state, donations and volunteers, working in association with the nearby historic railroad depot.

moments.title: Henniker
moments.text: Two stone arches carry Henniker’s Edna Dean Proctor Bridge across the Contoocook. Built in 1835, it belongs to the town’s water-powered industrial era, when mills on the river included a woolen factory. The mills closed in 1959 because of the Hopkinton-Everett Lakes Flood Control Project. The town’s school architecture also used stone: Henniker Academy’s building was constructed from split granite in 1836. Henniker is now home to New England College, while the river supports white-water kayaking. The main village sits where Route 114 meets Old Concord Road, along the same Contoocook River that powered its mills.

moments.title: Franklin Pierce Homestead
moments.text: The Franklin Pierce Homestead began beside a new turnpike. Benjamin Pierce bought land here and built the house in 1804, along with a tavern. It became the childhood home of Franklin Pierce, the future fourteenth president. The main block has a central hall downstairs and a ballroom across the front of the second floor. The family donated the property to New Hampshire in 1925, and restoration followed in the 1940s and 1960s. The barn has become a welcome center with displays and artifacts. Some original stenciled decoration survives inside the main block’s rooms.
